what: A Bloom filter is a tiny bit array that answers 'have I seen this?' with either 'definitely not' or 'probably yes'. It lets you skip expensive work for items that are surely absent.
like: Like a bouncer with a rough guest list: anyone not on it is surely turned away, but now and then a lookalike gets waved through.
why: Uses about 10 bits per item, far less than storing the items
Never says 'no' for something that is there - no false negatives
Cheap check in front of a slow disk read, network call or crawl

nodes.t: k hash functions|k positions per item

steps.d: Run the item through k hash functions. Each one points to a position in a bit array of m bits.
To add an item, switch those k bits to 1. The item itself is not stored, which is why the filter is so small.
To test an item, check its k bits. If any bit is 0, the item was never added - a sure no.
If every bit is 1, it is probably there, but other items may have set those bits. That is a false positive.
Only 'maybe' answers go on to the real, costly check, like reading an SSTable from disk or fetching a page.
RedisBloom gives you BF.RESERVE with a target error rate and capacity, then BF.ADD and BF.EXISTS from any service.

numbers.l: bits per item for a 1% false positive rate
hash functions that are optimal for a 1% error rate
extra per item cuts the false positive rate tenfold
Cassandra's default bloom_filter_fp_chance (0.1 for leveled compaction)
less memory with RocksDB's Ribbon filter, for more CPU

choices.d: Lower rates cost more bits: about 9.6 bits per item at 1%, about 14.4 at 0.1%. Pick by how expensive a wasted 'maybe' check is.
Size for the number of items you will add. Overfill a fixed filter and the false positive rate climbs fast.
The best k is about -ln(error rate) / ln 2, so 7 for 1%. Libraries usually work this out from your error rate.
RedisBloom adds sub-filters when full (expansion 2 by default). NONSCALING uses a bit less memory but errors once capacity is reached.
A plain Bloom filter cannot remove items. Use a counting Bloom filter or a cuckoo filter, or rebuild the filter on a schedule.

instead.why: A plain Redis set gives exact answers when memory is not tight
Caches the actual values, not just whether a key exists
Exact, durable membership lookups by key at any size
Uses Bloom filters inside each SSTable for you

breaks.d: More items than planned push most bits to 1.
breaks.see: False positive rate far above target; slow path hit far more often
breaks.fix: Size for real capacity, use a scaling filter, or rebuild bigger

breaks.d: Bits cannot be cleared without affecting other items.
breaks.see: Removed URLs or keys still pass the filter
breaks.fix: Counting Bloom or cuckoo filter, or a periodic rebuild

breaks.d: Code skips the real check on a 'maybe'.
breaks.see: Some new URLs are never crawled; some items wrongly marked seen
breaks.fix: Always confirm a maybe when a wrong yes matters

breaks.d: An in-memory filter disappears with the process.
breaks.see: Burst of slow-path work after a deploy
breaks.fix: Persist or rebuild it on startup, or keep it in Redis

say: For the crawler's seen-URL check I'll put a Bloom filter in front of the URL store: 'definitely not seen' means crawl, 'maybe' means check the store.
At a 1% false positive rate that is about 9.6 bits per URL with 7 hashes, so a billion URLs fit in roughly 1.2 GB.
It never gives a false negative, so we never skip a page we truly haven't crawled; a false positive just costs one extra lookup.
Cassandra and RocksDB use the same trick per SSTable, so a point read skips files that cannot hold the key.

followups.a: Adding an item sets all its k bits to 1, and bits are never cleared. So any added item will always find all its bits set. Only other items can accidentally set them, which gives false positives.
Bits per item is about -ln(p) / (ln 2)^2 and the best k is about -ln(p) / ln 2. For p = 1% that is about 9.6 bits and 7 hashes per item.

followups.q: How do LSM-tree databases use them?
followups.a: Each SSTable gets a Bloom filter in memory. A read checks the filter first and only opens files that might hold the key, saving disk reads for missing keys.
Use a counting Bloom filter, which keeps small counters instead of bits, or a cuckoo filter, which supports deletes and has better memory locality.

today: RocksDB also offers Ribbon filters, a Bloom alternative that saves about 30% of filter memory at the cost of 3-4x more CPU to build.

check.q: The filter says 'definitely not'. How sure is that?
check.a: Completely sure - it was never added
d: Sure only if the filter is small
It depends on the number of hashes
check.why: A 0 bit means the item never set it, so Bloom filters have no false negatives.

check.q: About how many bits per item for a 1% false positive rate?
You must remove items often. What fits best?
check.a: A cuckoo or counting Bloom filter
check.why: A plain Bloom filter cannot clear bits safely; these variants support deletes.

check.q: Why do Cassandra reads use Bloom filters?
check.a: To skip SSTables that cannot hold the key
check.why: Checking a small in-memory filter avoids opening files on disk for absent keys.
